items.title: What to expect from Apple's October 13 'Welcome home' releases
items.content_html:
Apple is releasing more hardware on October 13, with big expectations surrounding its smart home lineup. Here's what you can anticipate Apple will unveil, and what it probably won't.

For product launches, Apple is best known for its September special event, which is the venue for new iPhone models like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. However, it often holds more events in the fall than just one.

Regularly, it holds a second event in October or November, used to launch products that it didn't feel it could reveal alongside the iPhones. That is exactly the case for fall 2026.

Apple has confirmed that it will be holding a second fall event on October 13, 2026.Again, it will likely be a prerecorded presentation recorded at Apple Park, streamed on YouTube, the Apple TV app, and the Apple Event page. Some press will be in attendance in New York City.

This will be the second set of releases under the tenure of CEO John Ternus.

As usual, AppleInsider will be reporting in-depth about the product launches.

Apple launched a lot during its September 9 "Surprise and Shine" event, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and the fifth-generation AirPods.

That still leaves a lot of products waiting in the wings for an introduction. Based on rumors and expectations over the past few months, what follows is what you could expect Apple to bring out.

The most recent rumors regarding the event and Apple's plans include news of an unusual partnership with LG. The partnership will see Apple co-designed but LG-branded devices including a smart deadbolt lock, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera.

Despite this, Apple is said to still be working on its own range of smart home cameras. These are now expected to be launched in 2027.

Apple has also been working with Schneider to produce devices including smart thermostats, a humidity sensor, and more.

These are all new devices, but Apple is also expected to update its more familiar ranges such as Apple TV and HomePods.

HomePod mini - Likely

Starting off with the more probable launches, the HomePod mini is widely expected to get a refresh. Indeed, Apple's own code referenced new colors for the refreshed range.

The new models will retain the Blue, Black, and White colorways of the first-generation set, but Yellow and Orange are set to go. Instead, they will be replaced by Powder Pink and Forest Green.

An approximation of two new HomePod mini colors.

It won't just be a change in color, as it will almost certainly get a spec-bump update in the form of new chips. For the most part, the chip change will bring with it support for Siri AI, as well as some other features.

Other code leaks have referenced a new surround sound mode in a four-speaker setup. A "Party Mode" has also been mentioned, though not exactly what that means.

Apple TV 4K - Likely

Continuing the smart home theme, the Apple TV 4K is also expected to get a similar glow-up to the HomePod mini. Again, the main thrust of the change will be to introduce support for Siri AI, as one June code leak indicated.

The current expectations are an upgrade to the A19 or A19 Pro chip, as well as a possible upgrade of memory to 8GB or 12GB. The chip changes will also include the N1 networking chip, one of Apple's own design.

An Apple TV 4K and Siri Remote

While the design of the Apple TV 4K itself isn't expected to change this time around, there may be a new Siri Remote. Though product identifiers say a new controller is on the way, rumors are light on what will change.

Our best hope is for some form of ultra wideband or Find My integration for the Siri Remote.

Home Hub - extremely likely

Rounding out the smart home category, there is the often-rumored Home Hub. Or, at least, that's what we've been referring it as pre-launch.

Intended to be the center of a smart home setup, the Home Hub may take the form of half a HomePod with a display attached. A second version is one that could attach to a wall, possibly using a magnetic stand.

A mock-up of what the Home Hub could look like.

Effectively, it will be a smart display that shows a user's notifications, calendars, and other important daily details they need to know about. It will also handle tasks like FaceTime calls, using a built-in camera.

While a whole-home device, it will still maintain privacy in some way, such as checking for nearby iPhones or using AI. This should help it display information intended for a specific user, not to all home occupants.

The interface will apparently borrow ideas from the Apple Watch, including a home screen with "faces" and a "face gallery." This sounds like users will be able to set complications on the display that will be in view when not in active use.

It will also act as a central hub for your smart home, controlling Apple Home devices and being a central port of call for the network itself.

iPad mini - probably not

While it was a strong contender for launch alongside the iPhones, the iPad mini is still expected to get some form of update in 2026.

The eighth-generation device's main change is anticipated to be the display. An 8.4-inch LTPS panel with hybrid OLED should bring it in line with the iPad Pro range, if not to the same standard of specifications.

iPad mini on an arm

Beyond the display, you can also count on a chip upgrade. The current favorite is the A20, along with the possible inclusion of Apple's networking and modem chips.

Smaller changes that have been rumored include a repositioning of the FaceTime camera, as well as a new vibration-based speaker to help improve water resistance.

M6 MacBook Pro and iMac - Late October

A post-iPhone event is usually when Apple introduces new Mac products. However, following the surprise launches of the M6 Mac mini and updated Mac Studio in late August means there's fewer models for Apple to choose from.

The most obvious ones that have been rumored about are the M6 models. Catching up to the Mac mini, there are M6 models of MacBook Pro and iMac allegedly on the horizon.

The current 24-inch iMac.

The M6 MacBook Pro rumors say that it will still use a mini LED screen with ProMotion, the same six-speaker sound system, the same ports, and the same chassis as the current generation.

However, it will instead get an upgrade to the M6 chip, making it a typical Apple spec-bump upgrade.

It's a similar story for the M6 24-inch iMac, with it also thought to be given a speed boost, but retain the current design. An overhaul with OLED is expected for the iMac, but that will be far into the future.

OLED MacBook Pro - Late October

One of the big-hitter rumors for the MacBook Pro line has been the display. An OLED-equipped model has been rumored about for quite some time, and observers believe it could surface this time around.

While speculation put the launch in early 2027, it's now thought to take place in October. Or at least to be announced in October with a release in November.

An OLED display can offer richer black tones and a higher quality image for users, while also using less power. As a touchscreen, it will also be the first MacBook to be touch-enabled, and join a notebook market that already has many touch-enabled displays.

Other than the display, you can probably expect it to be a spec-bump update, including using Apple's newer chips. But there may be a change in construction that helps it lose weight.

On October 4, a report claimed there will be a significant weight reduction, thanks to Apple redesigning components to be smaller and lighter. Whether the weight loss will be enough to get closer to the lighter MacBook Air remains to be seen.

items.title: Perhaps obviously, iPhone Air 2 rumored to be significantly thinner than original
items.content_html:
Fairly obviously, the iPhone Air 2 is expected to adopt much of the iPhone Duo engineering, making it thinner. What's less obvious, is that the battery is expected to be at least as good.

That's according to a post on the Korean Naver blog by the familiar "yeux1122" account that has been responsible for multiple leaks in recent years.

If accurate, this news means that the iPhone Air 2 will measure around 5.2mm thick, compared to the iPhone Air's 5.6mm measurement. Notably, the iPhone Duo comes in at the same 5.2mm when open.

The prospect of a future iPhone Air becoming even thinner than the previous model isn't a surprise. But a previous report claiming an increased battery capacity makes this report all the more interesting.

Normally, making an iPhone thinner would mean reducing its battery capacity. But the leaker claims that won't be the case this time around.

"Battery capacity will actually increase (utilizing the high-density battery found in the "Pro" model,)" the report says via machine translation.

If that is indeed the case, it may be possible for Apple to increase battery capacity without increasing the dimensions of the original iPhone Air. But the suggestion that the iPhone Air 2 could be even thinner while boosting battery capacity is a different prospect entirely.

At this point, it's important to remember that this leaker has a mixed track record when it comes to pre-announced product details. With that in mind, while it's possible Apple's battery tech could make this all possible, we'd prefer the report to be backed up by another source.

The iPhone Air 2 is expected to be unveiled in early 2027, possibly alongside the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e.

items.title: Leaker doubles down on new iPad mini not having ProMotion
items.content_html:
A leaker with an average track record insists that the next iPad mini will have a 60Hz display, meaning it can't have the variable refresh rate that makes the device seem faster while helping battery life.

While rumors of an OLED iPad mini have been around since at least December 2024, most reports have predicted a launch by the end of 2026. A great many of those reports, though, have come from the same leaker, who is now also repeating their earlier claims about its display.

"Regarding the refresh rate of the Apple iPad mini OLED," leaker yeux1122 writes on Weibo. "There have been some mentions of 120Hz from overseas sources... however, it has already been confirmed that the domestic production units use LTPS."

By saying it will use LTPS, the leaker is stressing that the iPad mini will not have the LTPO technology needed for a variable refresh rate. "It is 60Hz — period," they conclude.

This 60Hz is the speed at which the screen refreshes, and it's significant because it's a fixed speed. The OLED displays on the iPad Pro can vary between 10Hz and 120Hz, which means they can speed up when needed.

So if you're watching a movie or playing a game, the screen — or even just part of it — will refresh faster and feel more responsive. If you're just reading a website, the screen slows down the refresh rate to save battery life.

This is called ProMotion, and if the leaker is correct, this forthcoming iPad mini will not have it. There is the fact that because it's OLED, it will be a higher-quality screen, but it's also probable that it won't be as bright as the display on the iPad Pro.

Separately, other reports have claimed that the new iPad mini may have the A20 Pro processor, as used in the iPhone 18 Pro.

items.title: iPad has competition from Amazon's new Alexa tablets
items.content_html:
Amazon is taking on Apple's iPad lineup with three new Alexa tablets that pack larger displays, built-in AI features, and prices starting at just $229.99.

The Alexa Tablet 8, Alexa Tablet 11, and Alexa Tablet 12 Pro feature aluminum bodies, upgraded displays, and built-in Alexa+ integration. Preorders opened October 8, with shipping scheduled to begin October 14.

Amazon's new tablets also replace the Fire OS software used on existing Fire tablets with Android and full Google Play Store access.

Customers can download popular apps such as YouTube, Netflix, Gmail, and Google Docs directly from Google's store. They won't need the workarounds previously required to install those apps on Fire tablets.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is the smallest and cheapest model at $229.99. Its 8.7-inch display sits inside an aluminum body weighing just 329 grams, making the tablet small enough for comfortable one-handed reading.

Amazon includes an eight-core processor, 4GB of RAM, 64GB of storage, and Wi-Fi 6 support. The company promises up to 14 hours of video playback, and a 128GB configuration is available for $279.99. Buyers can choose from Graphite, Rosette, and Teal.

The Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $329.99 with 64GB of storage, while the linked 128GB configuration costs $379.99. Both versions include 8GB of RAM, an eight-core processor, and an 11-inch 2.5K display with a 90Hz refresh rate.

Dual speakers with Dolby Atmos support handle audio, while Amazon rates battery life at up to 15 hours of video playback. The tablet also supports an optional $59.99 pen and a $79.99 keyboard case, with Graphite, Amethyst, and Matcha color options.

At the top of the lineup, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99 with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. It features a 12-inch 2.8K display with a 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio, giving users additional vertical space for documents and multitasking.

The larger tablet also includes a 4nm eight-core processor, Wi-Fi 6E, and four speakers supporting Dolby Atmos. Amazon claims up to 16 hours of video playback.

There's also a Nanomatte version with anti-glare glass developed alongside Corning. The entry-level Nanomatte configuration starts at $549.99 with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, while the linked 16GB RAM and 256GB model costs $679.99.

The Nanomatte display uses precision-etched glass to reduce reflections while preserving image detail. It's intended to make the screen easier to see in bright surroundings without relying on a conventional matte coating.

For anyone planning to use the 12 Pro for work, Amazon offers a $149.99 magnetic Pro Keyboard and an $89.99 Pro Pen. The keyboard includes a trackpad, while the stylus supports 4,096 pressure levels, tilt detection, and wireless charging.

The entry-level Tablet 8 and Tablet 11 configurations include sponsored lock-screen advertisements. Amazon also offers versions without the advertisements for an additional charge.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is closest in size to Apple's iPad mini, which starts at $599. Apple's 8.3-inch tablet uses the A17 Pro chip and supports Apple Pencil Pro, while Amazon's slightly larger 8.7-inch alternative costs $369 less.

Amazon's 11-inch model competes more directly with the standard iPad, which starts at $449. The Alexa Tablet 11 costs $119 less in its base configuration and offers a 90Hz display, compared with the iPad's 60Hz screen.

Apple's tablet uses the A16 chip and includes 128GB of storage at its starting price, twice the capacity of Amazon's cheapest 11-inch model.

Despite its Pro branding, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a closer comparison to the 13-inch iPad Air than the iPad Pro. Apple's M4-powered iPad Air starts at $949, compared with $499.99 for Amazon's regular 12 Pro.

Amazon offers a 120Hz display at the lower price, while Apple's iPad Air uses a 60Hz panel. The iPad Air also supports Apple Pencil Pro and Magic Keyboard, with access to Apple's iPadOS software and device ecosystem.

All three tablets include Alexa+, allowing customers to ask questions, control smart home devices, and interact with Amazon's assistant without leaving their current apps. Users can summon Alexa by voice or through an on-screen button.

An optional On-Screen Intelligence feature lets Alexa examine what's displayed and respond to questions about it. For example, customers can ask the assistant to compare products they're browsing or add dates from a displayed schedule to their calendar.

Amazon says screen access is disabled by default and must be enabled by the user. A visual indicator also appears whenever Alexa can see the display.

The tablets come with a free Alexa+ experience, so buyers don't need a Prime membership just to use the assistant on their new devices. A Prime membership or separate Alexa+ subscription is required for full access to Alexa+ across compatible Alexa and Echo devices.

Readers also get a dedicated Kindle mode that silences notifications, reduces blue light, and offers three display themes. Amazon claims battery life can reach 20 hours while reading.

All three Alexa tablets begin shipping October 14 in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Shipping to the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain begins October 19.

items.title: The Magic Mouse is 17 years old, it's time Apple fixed it
items.content_html:
The Magic Mouse will be 17 years old on October 20, 2026. It's beyond time Apple turned it from a curiosity into something that Mac owners actually want to use.

Apple officially unveiled the original Magic Mouse on October 20, 2009. It would ship with all iMacs, but existing Mac owners could buy one for $69.

At the time, Apple made a big thing about it being "the world's first multi-touch mouse," and it was right to. Remember, this was just two years after the iPhone introduced multi-touch to the world.

Ditching the buttons that were familiar to all computer users, the Magic Mouse had a single surface for users to tap. Tapping the left side initiated a left-click, with the right side becoming a right-click.

But the lack of buttons is what made the multi-touch possible. Gestures across the surface allowed Magic Mouse users to scroll content, swipe through timelines, and pan and zoom images.

This all sounds great, as it did 17 years ago. But there were problems and, with a refreshed model six years later, Apple's use of a belly-up charging setup made matters worse. Years later, Apple still hasn't addressed most of the issues putting people off buying a Magic Mouse.

Now, as the Magic Mouse hurtles towards yet another birthday, it's time that changed.

It's fair to say that for as futuristic and distinctly Apple as the Magic Mouse was, it was never universally liked. There was no native middle-click support, and gestures for some staple Mac OS X features were missing.

Other issues actually made the mouse unusable for some. Reports of Bluetooth instability affected some Macs more than others. Even if the mouse stayed connected, its low-profile design was uncomfortable for a lot of people.

This was perhaps the biggest drawback, and one that made the Magic Mouse an ergonomic nightmare. And this all happened a year before Apple design chief Jony Ive's form-over-function approach at least partially caused the iPhone 4's antennagate issue.

The Magic Mouse also used standard AA batteries. Apple even began selling its own rechargeable batteries and a charger to go with them.

It took Apple six years to add a built-in rechargeable battery.

Six years later, on October 13, 2015, the Magic Mouse 2 was announced alongside the Magic Trackpad 2. For the first time, a Space Gray option joined the standard White model, although it was initially only bundled with the iMac Pro. Yet more colors came with the M1 iMac refresh in 2021.

Apple made two main changes to the Magic Mouse 2, neither of which were well received.

Apple still hasn't moved its port

The addition of a rechargeable battery was initially welcomed. But Apple's decision to place the Lightning port on the bottom of the mouse is still mocked online to this day.

Apart from looking ridiculous, the port placement had a very real impact on usability. Being unable to use the mouse while charging it was a huge drawback, and one no other wireless mouse suffered from.

Apple also chose not to bring Force Touch from the Magic Trackpad 2 to the mouse. This was a problem for some who found that, because the whole surface of the mouse moved when clicking, it trapped their palm when it did.

The Magic Mouse 2 went unchanged until 2024, when Apple removed the Lightning port. Adding a USB-C port could have given Apple the chance to move it to a more traditional position, but it didn't.

So, here we are. We're uncomfortably close to the Magic Mouse's 17th birthday. It's basically the same mouse that went on sale in 2009, warts and all.

Apple could refresh the Magic Mouse at any moment, and I have to imagine that it will at some point. When it does, there are a few easy wins that I'd love to see Apple jump at.

The Magic Mouse is just uncomfortable to use

The most obvious fix would be to move the USB-C port to the edge of the mouse that cables normally protrude from. This is a solved problem, and every other mouse maker in the land knows it. It's time Apple got on board.

Apple may argue that a five-minute charge gives users enough juice to get through a full day of use. But that's an excuse for poor design, not a reason for it to remain that way.

I'd also like to see physical left and right buttons make a return to Apple's mouse. They're more ergonomic and add a tactility that the current whole-mouse-click situation doesn't afford.

That might mean Apple ditching the gestures that have made the Magic Mouse so magic to date, but not necessarily. The Logitech MX Master 4, for example, lets you press a button, then perform a gesture by moving the mouse itself.

Another quick win would be to remember that people use these things for more than five minutes at a time. The low-slung, smooth-like-a-dolphin approach looks great, but it makes for terrible ergonomics.

I'm genuinely curious whether anyone at Apple uses the Magic Mouse for any length of time each day. I doubt it. There's a reason every other mouse is shaped higher where it's gripped and lower at the buttons.

Unfortunately, all of these changes require the Magic Mouse to be completely redesigned. And that's probably why they won't happen.

But they absolutely should. And until they do, the Magic Mouse will always be a novelty that most iMac buyers throw in a drawer, never to see the light of day again.

items.title: Dumb down your Mac: Save 12GB by removing Apple Intelligence
items.content_html:
Mac users who don't want Apple Intelligence to take up precious drive space can free up capacity thanks to a new command-line tool.

Apple Intelligence is generally a good set of features for Apple's ecosystem of devices. However, not everyone particularly wants to use it.

That is especially a problem for Mac users with small drives and constrained spare capacity. For those stuck with a 256GB SSD, recovering 12GB can be extremely useful.

While the answer for this particular segment of Mac users would be to uninstall or remove Apple Intelligence, it's not that simple.

You can turn off Siri, but you can't delete the Apple Intelligence models in the macOS Settings at all.

Under macOS 27, there's no option to turn off Apple Intelligence at all. You can turn off Siri, but there's no single point in the menu to disable Apple Intelligence completely.

Even if you manage to disable Apple Intelligence, there's still data hanging around and no direct option to remove it. There are about 12 gigabytes of models that Apple Intelligence relies on, and that's storage users could find other uses for, if they were allowed to delete it.

Without a single Apple-sanctioned option to remove AI in the Settings, Mac users will have to look elsewhere for a solution.

A project by Om Lahore called RemoveMacAI aims to clean up your Mac of Apple Intelligence. It's a free project, released on GitHub under the MIT license.

RemoveMacAI is a script that installs a configuration profile to disable Apple Intelligence features on a Mac. That includes features like Siri AI, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, and more.

The start of running RemoveMacAI on a Mac mini.

As well as disabling features, it also removes the Apple Intelligence foundation models, as well as those for image generation, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up, and Xcode code completion.

The script's configuration profile works on restriction keys for Apple Intelligence, as well as for settings that don't have a restriction key. The models are removed using Apple's asset service, with System Integrity Protection enabled and System files kept intact.

Once deleted, the profile also redirects attempts to download each removed model to a closed local port. This prevents macOS from redownloading the models again.

However, you can remove the configuration profile to restore previous settings and allow the models to redownload.

AppleInsider recommends that users check out the project and ensure they are aware of what RemoveMacAI does before running it.

While there are a few ways to run RemoveMacAI, the easiest is from a single line, pasted into Terminal. At the time of publication, that line is:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash

Ran in Terminal, it downloads RemoveMacAI to a temporary folder and automatically runs. It shows how many features are active, how much storage space the models consume, and warns you about what happens if you proceed further.

At the prompt to "Turn Apple Intelligence off? [Y/N]" type Y, then enter.

A Device Management pop-up will appear, asking if you want to install the configuration profile. Click Install, and the script will continue to delete the models.

To revert the process, use this similar line in Terminal:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash -s revert

items.title: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Upgraded where it was needed
items.content_html:
The Apple Watch Series 12 is here, complete with a new Health Sensing System and more robust protection for its gorgeous display, making it the best non-Ultra Apple wearable yet.

Some Apple Watch updates are hard to distinguish from the previous model. Others bring design changes that are immediately obvious.

And then there's the Apple Watch Series 12.

A major redesign was unlikely for 2026, so the familiar look wasn't a surprise. That put more pressure on Apple to add features compelling enough to persuade current owners to upgrade.

The Apple Watch Series 12 adds several new features, but even smaller upgrades can make a noticeable difference in everyday use. Those changes deserve a closer look.

Apple also released the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for those who want a more rugged smartwatch. But for most people, the Apple Watch Series 12 offers everything they need.

At first blush, the Apple Watch Series 12 looks identical to the outgoing Apple Watch Series 11. But there are differences, most notably in the materials and colors on offer.

Like most recent releases, the Apple Watch Series 12 is available in 42mm and 46mm case sizes. Aluminum and titanium options remain, and ceramic has returned.

Apple Watch Series 12 review: A familiar look

Most buyers will likely choose the entry-level aluminum model on review here. It comes in four colors: dark bronze, light gold, black, and Space Gray.

The titanium model comes in gold and natural, while the ceramic model comes in pearl white and night blue.

Beyond the case materials and colors, the Apple Watch Series 12 has two main design changes. One is on the front, and the other is on the back.

The front of the Apple Watch Series 12 gets a durability upgrade that matters if you're rough on your watch. For the first time, the aluminum model features Ceramic Shield 2.

Apple says the upgraded protection is 60% tougher than the Ion-X glass previously used on aluminum Apple Watches. It's still too early to know how well that claim will hold up to daily use.

The other change is the new Health Sensing System, found on the back of the new Apple Watch. Replacing the previous sensors, the new addition promises more frequent and accurate readings.

The change is obvious when you first turn the Apple Watch Series 12 over. The new sensor array features larger electrodes situated around the photodiodes that collect data from the wrist.

Some of the Apple Watch Series 12's biggest features fall under the Audio Intelligence label. They aren't available yet and won't arrive until mid-to-late October 2026.

The Apple Watch Series 12 still includes the familiar features of earlier models. That means health and fitness tracking, sleep monitoring, and an App Store full of apps.

Interchangeable bands are still a key feature of the Apple Watch, and the always-on display is a great way to use apps and enjoy colorful, data-rich watch faces. But even beyond the health features that have built up over the years, this model still ups the ante.

With Apple Watch Series 12, Apple has added the Readiness score to its suite of health features. It uses your health and vitals data to calculate a new score each morning and update it throughout the day.

The idea of a readiness rating isn't new, and we've seen similar features on smart rings and other wearables before. But this is Apple's first attempt.

Apple Watch Series 12 review: New sensors for 2026

The theory is a simple one. Apple uses the Readiness score to give Apple Watch wearers an idea of whether they should push their body or take a rest.

This is especially useful for athletes, both professional and casual, who may want to maximize performance while minimizing injury risk.

The new Health Sensing System also takes heart rate measurements more frequently. The Apple Watch Series 12 measures your heart rate every five seconds and heart rate variability (HRV) every five minutes.

As part of the Health Sensing System's new additions, Recovery HRV analyzes your HRV overnight for the first time. This data can help identify stress and recovery, and helps Apple build the Readiness score.

Battery life has always been a key factor for Apple Watch buyers. Improvements in recent years have made it easier to wear overnight for sleep tracking.

With Apple Watch Series 12, Apple has maintained the 24-hour battery life of its predecessor. That extends to 38 hours when using Low Power Mode.

It still charges to 80% in about 30 minutes, but the most notable improvement comes in the first 15 minutes.

Apple says a 15-minute charge provides the Apple Watch Series 12 with enough juice to run for a full 12 hours. A five-minute charge is enough for 10 hours of sleep tracking.

This works fine enough now. I'm a little concerned what happens when the battery capacity starts deteriorating, but we'll see about that in a year or so.

Those charging speeds make a quick top-up enough to keep the Apple Watch Series 12 running. You don't need a full charge to get through the day or track your sleep overnight.

Audio Intelligence is one of the biggest additions to Apple's 2026 watches. It includes four features, but two aren't available yet.

Apple Watch Series 12 review: Siri is listening

The two features that we do have aren't strictly new. Sound Recognition was already available as an accessibility feature, alerting people to alarms, doorbells, and sirens.

Music Recognition is still Shazam, but now it's part of the Smart Stack for easier access. Not Earth-shattering, by any stretch of the imagination.

But Live Rewind and Siri Recap are different. Both caused a stir when they were announced.

Live Rewind is the less useful of the two features, though it can help when you miss something someone just said. Double-pressing the Digital Crown turns the last 15 seconds of captured audio into text.

Siri Recap works similarly but covers conversations throughout the day. It takes notes on conversations the Apple Watch hears, creating a running record.

If you're worried about Siri Recap recording your conversations, you're not alone. Yet, Apple stresses that it only runs when you ask it to.

Apple also points out that Siri Recap doesn't record or save audio. Instead, Apple Intelligence generates summaries based on what it hears and deletes those summaries after seven days.

Apple says Siri Recap doesn't identify who said what. It summarizes the conversation without naming individual speakers.

Personally, I think Siri Recap could be hugely useful for someone who, like me, suffers from the inattentive flavor of ADHD. I can forget the gist of a conversation almost as soon as it ends.

But, again, I haven't been able to test how Siri Recap or Live Rewind actually work. Until I can, it's impossible to really understand their abilities, limitations, and perhaps legal restrictions on recording without the other parties' permissions.

More on this in the future, though.

Audio Intelligence aside, and having used and tested what's available today, the Apple Watch Series 12 is the best non-Ultra Apple Watch yet. As was the Series 11 before it. And the Series 10 before that.

The fact that these updates are iterative is one that's hard to escape, but the iterations are all worthwhile. The new Health Sensing System is welcome, as is Ceramic Shield 2 on the aluminum models.

Apple Watch Series 12 review: Apple's specs sheet

The S11 chip keeps apps responsive and supports Apple Intelligence features. The new colors look good, and ceramic is a welcome addition to the lineup.

Ultimately, if you're in the market for a new Apple Watch, the Series 12 is easy to recommend. Unless you're an outdoorsy type, in which case the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the better bet.

For current Apple Watch owners, the decision to upgrade may depend on Audio Intelligence. Its performance and usefulness will help determine whether the Series 12 is worth buying.

It's impossible to know right now, so my recommendation is simple: new buyers should buy the latest model. Owners of the Apple Watch Series 11 should wait and see what the new features bring.

Unless you really want that ceramic finish, of course. And I definitely can't blame you if you do.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, but retailers are already discounting the wearable by as much as $50 at the time of this review.

items.title: Meta's Muse is now on the iPad App Store. Leave it there.
items.content_html:
Muse, the AI agent from Facebook parent company Meta, is now available as a native iPad app and unfortunately, some people are going to download it.

If you need to read any further than the words Meta or Facebook, this is the situation:

Meta Muse is an AI agent you can tell not to read your private information, but of course it will anyway.

On macOS, this is why Apple is changing how users can allow apps to access everything on the Mac. Amazon has blocked Muse from buying anything on its platform.

Now it's on the iPad — link if you really must — although so far only in the US. It's the same with the iPhone version, which has already gathered 173,000 ratings.

Those ratings average out at 4.9 stars. Although one praising review includes the line that "no way all this should be free," which just tells you people never learn.

It's not as if they haven't had any warning that Meta wants private information. Apple has singled out the company for using EU regulations to request access to far more personal detail than its services ever require, for instance.

Or there's how Facebook renamed itself Meta since even it knew the original name was tainted. Facebook is the firm that sold Cambridge Analytica access to the data of around 87 million users, and got fined $725 million over it.

Cambridge Analytica went bust, but Facebook/Meta continues. More recently, Meta launched what it calls Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses and everyone else calls "pervert glasses."

Meta does have an online privacy statement that of course leans heavily on how it won't do anything without your permission. But then it has a page on how Muse works, and there it says "no automated system is perfect," before adding that "you're responsible for fixing errors."

Maybe you don't have a problem with a corporation saying it's up to you to correct problems. Perhaps you're not concerned about your personal data being gathered and sold.

If that's because you think it's just your name and maybe your date of birth, look what happened when Apple stepped in with App Tracking Transparency. Facebook had to tell investors that its revenues were going to be down $10 billion for the year, just because of that one move.

Meta profits heavily from what it learns about you, which is why it can be free.

But then even if you're not concerned about Meta making a fast buck as long as it's providing you with a service, take a look at what else Muse is doing. Through your contacts and messages, it is harvesting data about everyone you ever deal with.

Ask them if their privacy is worth your being able to have Muse automatically reschedule a meeting for you.

items.title: How Apple's M6 chip gets more performance at a smaller scale
items.content_html:
A close look at the M5 and M6 chips reveals big changes in design at the 2-nanometer level, allowing Apple to significantly improve the performance of the M6.

The M6 introduced with the Mac mini in August is the first desktop-class Apple chip using a 2-nanometer fabrication process. The change, which means Apple can make the chips denser, has resulted in big improvements in terms of performance.

Die shots posted to YouTube by High Yield and SemiAnalysis offer a glimpse into the changes Apple made to the chip's design.

The die shrink means there's a physical difference in size between the generations. The M5 is made on a 12.75mm by 12.08mm sliver of silicon, occupying 154 square millimeters, using TSMC's N3P process node.

The M6 is much smaller, at 12.8mm by 11.06mm, giving it only 141.6 square millimeters to play with. However, since it uses the N2 process node, it can fit more into a smaller space.

The analysis points out that while there's some similarities between the M5 and M6 layouts, there are many differences. The first obvious similarity is the memory interface, which is arranged at the top of each die.

The 16GB DRAM model of the M6 has the same 9,600 megatransfer per second DRAM as the M5, giving it the same memory bandwidth. The 24GB and 32GB memory M6 models have the increased 170GB/s memory bandwidth due to using faster 10,667-megatransfers DRAM instead.

A GPU cluster is located below the memory, but with the M6 having a clearly different structure due to having two more GPU cores on hand. However, the die shrink also means the GPU cores on the M6 are about 10% smaller than the M5.

Below that is the same 16-megabytes of System Level cache across both generations.

We already knew Apple changed the CPU section, with Apple moving from four super cores and six efficiency cores in the M5 to two super, four performance, and six efficiency cores in the M6.

Looking at the M6 die shot, the two S-cores are quite large, similar to the M5, and each have their own slice of L2 cache, too. That cache is also larger, at 1.5 megabytes per core.

The new M6 S-cores are, again, smaller than the M5 versions, even with their individual L2 caches being 50% larger.

Die maps of the M5 [left] and M6 [right] - Image Credit: High Yield, SemiAnalysis/YouTube

That said, the two cores are also connected to two large shared L2 caches, but it's unusual in design. Both shared caches are 10 megabytes in size, which is a combined 4 megabytes more than on the M5.

However, one appears to be made with an 80-kilobyte SRAM macro, referring to blocks of memory.

While Apple has also reduced the super core count in favor of more performance cores, the four P-cores are connected to those same shared caches. It's a combined cluster, rather than the cache being limited to just one of the two core types.

The efficiency or E-core cluster is still separate, just like the M5. The M6 version is, again, arranging six cores around 8 megabytes of shared cache, up 2 megabytes from the M5.

Apple also includes an AMX unit for the E-core cluster. This refers to the Apple Matrix Coprocessor, used to help with matrix math.

As seen with the A20 Pro, Apple's Neural Engine is now double in size when it comes to core counts. However, rather than being jammed into whatever space was available on the A20 Pro, the M6 version takes a more symmetrical approach.

Shown in the die shot as a sideways T, the cores are shown to be split into two clusters, each made up of eioght dual-core sections. The two sides have their own caches, before converging in a central control area.

Along the bottom, the I/O of the chip hasn't changed much, but there are some PCI-Express lanes, specifically the physical layers (PHYs).

There are the same four-lane display PHY as well as a seven-lane camera PHY. But the high-speed PHY lanes are shown to use the same designs across all six of the PCI-Express lanes.

The PHY lanes for PCI-Express also appear to be the same as the ones used for Thunderbolt PHYs. The analysis believes this could be six lanes of PCI-Express Gen 4.

This is a big improvement over the M5, which used three lanes of PCI-Express Gen 4 and two more of PCIe Gen 3.

The current belief is that the M6 generation will be a shorter one than usual, with Apple expected to move to the AI-centric M7 within months. There will almost certainly be more changes to the chip designs for that generation.

The analysis proposes that a big one will be Apple changing the memory interface. It's been the same 128-bit interface it's used since the M1.

The A20 and A20 Pro hint at this as a possibility, as each use a wide 96-bit interface. Since the M-series chips are fundamentally based on their mobile counterparts, this could be a change coming along with the next generation.

items.title: Texas school district turns to Apple as Chromebook repair costs skyrocket
items.content_html:
Aging Chromebooks and mounting repair costs are a driving force behind one Texas school district switching to iPad and Apple's more economical over time MacBook Neo.

Beaumont Independent School District's board approved a four-year, $11.19 million lease for 14,585 Apple devices. The district expects annual payments of about $2.8 million to replace aging equipment used by students and teachers.

The lease, reported by Beaumont Enterprise, includes 4,085 iPads for pre-K through second grade and 9,500 MacBook Neos for older students. Teachers within the school district will receive 1,000 MacBook Neo laptops under the agreement.

Deputy superintendent Rachel Harrah said nearly two-thirds of the district's devices are beyond their recommended life cycle. The district reported more than 6,600 repairs last year and spent nearly $470,000 in repair and support costs across several reporting periods.

Currently, the district primarily uses Chromebooks. Harrah has said current devices are becoming increasingly difficult to repair, with replacement part costs well over $100 per piece in some cases.

"It's almost half a million dollars just supporting a fleet that is barely moving or working," said Harrah.

Additionally, the district is trying to be more forward-thinking. It would rather students get practical experience on devices that are used within the workplace.

"There is not one environment in the workplace that uses a Chromebook," Harrah said.

The district also compared MacBook Neo with Lenovo and Asus models, reporting lower four-year costs for Apple's option. Harrah pointed to 0% laptop financing, 0.99% iPad financing, AppleCare+ access, and potential resale proceeds as reasons for her recommendation.

The first payment will come from district reserves, with later payments drawing on existing revenue and replacement budgets. Officials plan to evaluate the devices after four years and could postpone replacement if their condition allows.

items.title: Apple's escalating crackdown on ad vendors is catching some innocent victims
items.content_html:
When iOS 27 was released, a legit advertising company found it could no longer serve ads to the Safari browser. This block appears to be a mistake on Apple's side, but the ad industry is up in arms about the implications.

Apple introduced App Tracking Transparency back in 2021 in order that users had to choose to allow ad companies to track them using identifiers. After a heavy initial impact, though, the rates of users allowing tracking has risen again, and advertisers have found alternative ways to learn about users.

However, according to advertising trade journal AdExchanger, The Trade Desk ad agency was blocked in iOS 27 by Apple itself. It appears that Apple is intentionally blocking data brokers who sell on tracked data, but in doing so it prevented The Trade Desk serving ads.

The Trade Desk filed a bug report that surmised that the "intent seems to be to hard block domains that power 'post-cookie' identity." However, the affected addresses include the company's "ad request and delivery domain, not identity [tracking]."

This is the system where The Trade Desk, or any other vendor like Google, bids on ad space in real-time as a page loads for the user. If it wins that bid, the company then serves an ad to the web browser based on what the ad vendor thinks it knows about the viewer. This is not in itself about tracking individual users.

So far this sounds like a mistake on Apple's part, and that appears to have been backed up by how the block on The Trade Desk has effectively been removed. However, it is only removed in iOS 27.2, which so far is solely in beta testing.

That means The Trade Desk still cannot serve ads to Safari, and will remain blocked from doing so until iOS 27.2 ships.

Curiously, it also appears that Apple's new moves include the aim of having a dynamic block list. So in future, without having to wait for a new iOS update, Apple could elect to block or unblock specific advertisers.

It's not clear why that isn't happening right now with The Trade Desk.

What does appear to be clear is that iOS 27 blocked a number of firms in Safari. Since that really means they were blocked in WebKit, those firms are also shut out of Chrome or any other browser on iOS.

AdExchanger claims to have had sight of a list of ad tech firms that Apple either is or may target. Reportedly, it includes hundreds of firms, but allegedly that may not include Google.

While it's still supposition, the idea that Google is not blocked is backed up by The Trade Desk's bug report. The Trade Desk claims to have logs of its advertising bids being blocked while Google's went through as normal.

Apple has not made any announcements about its iOS 27 advertising identity blocking, nor is it expected to. But it does fit with how the company adds privacy protections that advertisers then continually work to circumvent.

Since the introduction of App Tracking Transparency in 2021, that has meant advertisers looking for ways to gain more information about users. One way involves this bidding process, which can mean advertisers being told details such as how many people are expected to see the ad.

The advertising industry wants as much information about users as it can get, and Apple wants to protect users' privacy as much as it can. Up to now, that may have made advertisers unhappy, but it was intended to help users.

It has instead drawn the ire of Meta, for one. And, many antitrust investigations have sprung up about it.

Today, though, Apple is expanding its own advertising business, with ads in Apple Maps, and soon perhaps in Visual Intelligence.

Consequently, advertisers are concerned about Apple having the facility to turn off ads from its rivals. That seems unlikely, though, as it would doubtlessly lead to antitrust lawsuits, and Apple is embroiled in enough of those already.

items.title: Design is a Jobsian-level focus for John Ternus
items.content_html:
John Ternus is putting his stamp on Apple by focusing on the company's design work, with the CEO taking an almost Jobsian approach to make design great again.

The era of Tim Cook as Apple CEO was one of growth, with sales and manufacturing the core of his tenure at the top. Under the rule of Ternus, design is becoming a top priority once more for the company, as Ternus aims to add more to the company by strengthening its weaker areas.

Writing in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman writes about a conversation between Ternus and Cook, and how Ternus needed to be himself as CEO instead of emulating Cook. To Ternus, it was an apparent turning point.

Cook had spent his tenure as CEO working on where he could generate "the most value for Apple," Ternus told employees. Therefore, Ternus believed he had to do the same, while still being himself.

The result is that areas Cook focused on, such as financial strategy and the supply chain, are being handled by CFO Kevan Parekh and COO Sabih Khan. Ternus, who is very much an engineer, is instead working closely with chief hardware officer Johny Srouji and hardware engineering leader Tom Marieb.

At the same time, he's also taking a lot more time to look at design, which has fallen behind since the departure of Jony Ive in 2019. There were leaders working for the industrial design and human interface design groups, but they were separate rather than a single executive covering both areas.

Those leaders also reported to former COO Jeff Williams, who had a background in manufacturing but not design. When Williams retired in 2025, those teams were said to be reporting directly to Cook instead.

That wasn't for long, as Cook handed the responsibility for design to Ternus ahead of the CEO transition. During the transition itself, the design chiefs were effectively the only direct reports Ternus had before taking the top spot at the company.

Ternus has previous experience working with the design studio, in his role as head of hardware engineering. After becoming CEO, he has become even closer to the design teams, and has reportedly worked hands-on in the studio numerous times a week.

This is a stark contrast to Cook, who very much focused on the other areas of the company that he knew best. Cook only visited the studio for about an hour once a month, the report said.

Cook's arms-reach approach to design was also a big departure from his predecessor, Steve Jobs. Jobs was famous for being deeply involved with design, which Ternus seems to be emulating.

Raising the profile of design at Apple is a tough task, especially following the departure of Ive. Part of this is actually from Ive's design studio, LoveFrom, taking some of the design team out of the company.

Apple's design leads Steve Lemay (left) and Molly Anderson, during the iPhone Duo launch - image credit: Apple.

There have also been losses to OpenAI's hardware team and other tech firms, thinning the studio's ranks. Then there's the departures of software design leader Alan Dye and industrial design chief Evans Hankey exiting to OpenAI.

The current VP of Industrial Design, Molly Anderson, didn't have a high profile, and also hadn't managed a team as large as Apple's before taking the role. But even so, Gurman says that there's no search happening for an external chief design officer.

Instead, there has been an effort by Apple to shore up what it already has and to rebuild. That has included bringing Anderson and Dye successor Steve Lemay to the fore with the launch of the iPhone Duo, as well as hiring more designers for its team.

Apple may not be searching for someone to take control over the design teams right now. Considering the amount of attention for design he has at the moment, Ternus may believe he can do it himself.

items.title: This Wi-Fi eGPU for Mac sounds good in theory, if you can afford it
items.content_html:
The WiCi One is a wireless GPU that can handle AI tasks and even gaming graphics rendering for your Mac over a network. We have questions.

The graphics processing unit (GPU) is an important part of everyday computing. Doing everything from handling graphics for games to processing AI tasks locally.

For users of small computers incapable of holding a full-size graphics card, such as a thin notebook or a compact computer, an option is an external GPU enclosure.

However, that brings with it a bunch of other issues. No one with a notebook wants to keep their thin and portable device connected to a large box using a Thunderbolt cable all the time.

The WiCi One is trying something different. While it is an external GPU, it's one that is instead designed to work over a wireless network.

The ides is that the WiCi One is a computer on your home network, packing a beefy GPU. A Mac or PC could then access the power of that GPU over the network to handle a variety of tasks.

That can include locally processed AI and models using Ollama, LM Studio, Hugging Face, and PyTorch. The GPU can also be harnessed to handle video rendering in Premiere Pro and CapCut, or 3D rendering for Maya, AutoCAD, or Blender.

There's also the possibility of using it for gameplay, with WiCi claiming it can even drive the graphics in games like Cyberpunk 2077. And the company says this is all done by the unit acting as a local GPU over Wi-Fi.

Inside the WiCi One is one of two configurations, with the base one being an Nvidia RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB of DDR7. That's running alongside an Intel Core 3 100U processor and 1TB of NVMe 4 storage.

The upper-tier model is fitted with a beefier Nvidia RTX 5090 with 32GB of GDDR7 memory, along with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H processor and 4TB of NVMe 5 storage. While it does have a processor, the WiCi One is designed to act just as a GPU source, not as a server in its own right.

WiCi One exploded view - Image Credit: WiCi

So, in essence, this is a Intel server, with a Nvidia GPU inside.

When it comes to performance, the company claims high performance when it comes to AI work. That includes an AI compute capability of about 420 FP16 TFLOPS for the 5090 edition, and 95 for the 5060 Ti.

An M5 Max Mac Studio is claimed to reach about 70TFLOPS by comparison.

For holding AI models in memory, the WiCi One takes advantage of the NVMe SSD for paging with TurboStream. On the Mac Studio, the comparison is with the memory, between 36GB and 128GB.

The ability hold large models is also another advantage, with the WiCi One capable of holding Kimi K3 with 2.8 trillion parameters. The 36GB memory of the Mac Studio is estimated to hold 70 billion parameters.

This is all packed into a compact chassis that WiFi claims has a quiet thermal design. It's an item that could theoretically sit on a shelf, out of the way, instead of on a desk somewhere.

Networking is handled by a Wi-Fi 7 radio with 4x4 MIMO, 320MHz of bandwidth, and twin antennas to minimize latency. It's described by WiCi as having "Router-grade AirLink Multi-Link transport."

The use of Wi-Fi sounds like a bad idea compared to a connection like Thunderbolt. However, Wi-Fi 7 has a maximum theoretical bandwidth of 48Gbps under optimal conditions, which should be more than enough for an eGPU to function.

And, there hasn't been Thunderbolt eGPU support, much less modern Nvidia drivers, on Apple hardware for years.

Theoretical being the main word there, as real-world connectivity will be much less than that.

The back of the WiCi One, with unmentioned Ethernet - Image Credit: WiCi

WiCi is certainly marketing it as a wireless-forward device, to the point that it doesn't mention any alternative connections on its website. However, press images show there may be an Ethernet connection and either a USB-C or Thunderbolt port on the rear.

All of these claims make the WiCi One an interesting choice for gamers who want to play on a MacBook Pro, but especially for those who are working in the field of AI.

Considering how expensive cloud-based AI services can get for heavy users, a high-end local processing solution is a viable option.

With Apple promoting its Mac Studio as an AI powerhouse, this is precisely the kind of market that the WiCi One is taking on. That goes for the premium pricing too.

The WiCi One starts with a list price of $2,599 for the 5060 Ti model, rising to $9,999 for the 5090 model. Both are being sold with a $600 discount for early buyers, bringing the prices down to $1,999 and $9,399 respectively.

For reference, the M5 Max Mac Studio starts from $2,499, with the M5 Ultra from $5,499.

AppleInsider will be finding out whether it lives up to its wireless claims as part of a review of the WiCi One soon.

items.title: uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: Halfway between AI powerhouse and basic NAS
items.content_html:
At $1,449.99, six hard drive bays in the uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra, coupled with dual 10GbE and Thunderbolt are the real draw, not its AI billing.

A NAS lives or dies on two things. One is how much it can contain, the other is how fast you can move it.

uGreen's DXP6800 Ultra bets hard on the second. It piles on connectivity that pricier rivals often charge extra for.

The "Ultra" name and uGreen's AI marketing invite scrutiny. The chip inside tells a more modest story.

So the real draw here is input and output. This is a fast, expandable box, not an AI powerhouse. Fortunately, it's not priced badly based on marketing buzzwords.

A six-bay NAS cannot hide what it is. This is a boxy metal tower built to hold drives.

Six lockable bays load from the front. Two M.2 slots sit inside for cache or SSD pools.

It measures about 11.6 by 10.2 by 7.4 inches. This is a device for a shelf, not a desk.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: The rear has a dust guard for the fans.

Power draw is modest for the class. uGreen rates it at 43 watts during drive access. We saw a bit more at 60W when the unit was under load, and getting slammed with I/O requests at the same time.

For the testing suite, we tested the unit with six 2TB Seagate Red drives provided by Ugreen. We also used four 24TB WD Red Pro, that retail for $1059 per drive on Amazon.

SSDs used for testing included a pair of Samsung 990 Evo Plus drives, and a pair of Samsung SSD 9100 Pro 1TB drives. You don't need to use drives this fast. Stick with PCI-E 3.0 drives if you have them, as they're cheaper, and still provide more than enough speed.

Here is where the "Ultra" badge needs a closer look. The chip is an Intel Core 5 120U.

It has 10 cores and 12 threads, up to 5.0GHz. That is capable, but not cutting-edge.

The part is based on Intel's older Raptor Lake design. Crucially, it has no dedicated NPU.

That matters, because uGreen markets this line on AI. On-device AI runs on the CPU here, not a Neural Engine.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: The front port selection

For photo tagging and search, it still works fine. It just will not fly like the uGreen NASync iDX6011 does, and heavy AI is a stretch. That's fine, though.

For normal NAS duties, the chip more than beefy enough. File serving, Docker, and streaming are easy work.

As a reference, the older Geekbench 6 benchmarking suite puts it near 1,750 single-core. Multi-core lands around 6,200. For reference the M1 Mac mini has a 2191 single-core score, and a 8576 multi-core.

This is not really a handicap for the hardware class, though. Beyond file sharing, combined with 8GB of ECC RAM, as shipped, this still is a good machine for Docker, and apps natively running on the hardware.

ECC support is rare at this price. We're not going to get into it, but the longer something runs, the more likely it is to get a bit flipped now and again from ionizing radiation, or just a random error. ECC guards against that.

Memory can be expanded to 96GB for heavier work, assuming you have the budget for it. What it ships with is ample for most SOHO Docker and virtual machine needs.

The six bays are the whole point of a six-bay NAS. Each takes a SATA drive up to 32TB.

Two M.2 NVMe slots add fast storage. I think they're best used for cache, but uGreen allows that, or for or a separate SSD storage pool.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: The front-accessible drive bays

uGreen lists a maximum capacity of 208TB. That combines six 32TB drives with two NVMe sticks.

RAID spans JBOD, Basic, and RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10. That covers speed and redundancy alike.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: The hatch for accessing the M.2 section

A separate 128GB SSD holds the system, and is not user accessible. It keeps UGOS Pro off your main array.

On a gigabit Ethernet network, a single spinning hard drive can and will saturate what's available for wired bandwidth. Properly configured, and fully populated a striped RAID of hard drives will saturate a 10-gig network.

As always, we're very pleased with uGreen network speeds. There are no artificial slowdowns and it is always external network load slowing down transfer speeds.

This is where the DXP6800 Ultra earns its name. The connectivity is generous.

There are two 10GbE Ethernet ports, not one. With the right networking hardware, they can serve fast network access. Speeds will still be limited to 10 gigabits per second per client, mostly because of client speeds.

Two Thunderbolt 4 ports sit on the front. Each offers up to 40Gbps to a connected Mac.

The Thunderbolt 4 ports are primarily intended to ingest data from other drives and store it locally. They can be used to expand storage too, if you need.

You can also use them to network over Thunderbolt with another computer, but only up to as fast as 10 gigabits. To say it plainly, the NASync DXP6800 is not a Drobo DAS replacement, which is unfortunate.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: The rear port selection

A PCIe Gen4 x4 slot adds real expansion. Few NAS boxes at this price include one. This is a major selling point for the unit.

The rest covers 8K HDMI for configuration or media playback, 10gbit/sec USB-A, and an SD 4.0 reader. There is little a creative desk would miss.

The 10GbE ports need matching network gear to shine. The faster copper networking is still rare in SOHO environments, but implementation is ticking up.

The DXP6800 Ultra runs UGOS Pro. The software has matured, though it trails Synology.

If you need it for backups, there's support for Time Machine, though it's not immediately usable. We're not going to get into the procedure here, but UGreen has a video about it. The support document is a bit better, though.

While it once wasn't, UGOS Pro is easy to set up, easy to manage, and easy to control access.

The onboard software options are what you'd expect from a typical NAS. You have your private image album library system, your video storage and playback tools, and other productivity-centric items.

If you're into downloading large files legitimately via Bittorrent, there's a tool built in for just that, but you can install more if you want.

But, with all of this performance on tap, eventual users may want to do more. Thankfully, there's Docker support, so you can install an array of different network services on the NAS.

Don't like Docker? You can also run virtual machines on it instead.

With the performance of the chip used here, those services will be quick enough.

But remember the missing NPU from earlier. These features lean on the CPU, so temper expectations.

Docker support opens the usual self-hosting options. Plex and Jellyfin both run here. A Plex container managed to serve six concurrent 4K streams, while transcoding.

UGOS Pro is also not the only choice. The x86 hardware can run TrueNAS or Unraid instead, which is beyond the scope of this review.

uGreen's NAS range has become crowded. The DXP6800 Ultra needs placing carefully.

Below it sits the four-bay DXP4800 Pro. That model has fewer bays, one 10GbE port, and no Thunderbolt.

uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra review: PCI-E expansion

Above it sits the AI-focused IDX6011 Pro. That one carries the real NPU hardware.

The choice comes down to priorities. For bays and I/O, this is the pick.

Want serious on-device AI instead? Spend more for the IDX6011 Pro.

The DXP6800 Ultra is easy to sum up. It is a generous six-bay NAS with standout connectivity.

Dual 10GbE, Thunderbolt 4, and a PCIe slot rarely appear together. At this price, that bundle is the real value.

The "Ultra" and AI billing oversells the hardware, a bit. A no-NPU Raptor Lake part is not an AI engine.

Judge it on storage and I/O, and it shines. Judge it on AI, and it falls short.

For a Mac creative wanting fast shared storage, it fits well. Maybe the next one can be used as direct attached storage over Thunderbolt.

From humble beginnings, to mature software now, unfettered by unrealistic restraints, uGreen has turned into our favorite NAS vendor. There are no drive lock-downs, there's hardware transcoding, and an excellent feature set for the price.

And now, there's something for everybody in the line from basic backup server to AI powerhouse, hitting every rung in between. It's been fun to watch this product line mature since our first uGreen NAS review, and I'm extremely glad that they're making a run at Synology for market champion.

The uGreen NASync DXP6800 Ultra is available from Amazon for $1,449.99 at retail pricing. Watch for sales.

Members of the public should seek out the public betas instead of the developer versions. They are much safer alternatives if you want to try out prerelease software.

items.title: Mac mini M5 Pro review: Mini gets serious, with one caveat
items.content_html:
In the tale of two 2026 Mac minis, there is a more "Pro" oriented one, but as with the Mac Studio, it's a complicated tale to tell.

The gap between the two Mac minis in 2026 is wider than you'd think at first glance. Like the Pro model before it, the M5 Pro Mac mini has Thunderbolt 5, far more cores, and faster memory.

It also adds a lot to the price. At $1,699, it edges toward Mac Studio territory. It's a great computer, but it's hard to recommend when you start adding upgrades.

The M5 Pro Mac mini shares the compact M4 design. It is a 5-inch square, 2 inches tall.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: same compact design

It weighs 1.6 pounds, just over the base model. The extra likely reflects a bigger cooler.

The front carries two 10gbit USB-C ports and a headphone jack. The power button still sits underneath.

Nothing about the outside signals the Pro chip. You buy this one for what is inside.

The M5 Pro is the reason this mini exists. It is both a jump and a side-step from the M6 Mac mini.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: a pro chipset in a tiny computer

The base chip has a 15-core CPU, with five super cores and ten performance cores. An 18-core CPU is available for more money.

The GPU runs 16 cores, or 20 if upgraded.

Memory bandwidth is the standout number. At 307GB/s, it dwarfs the base mini's figure.

Geekbench results show the muscle.

M5 Pro Mac mini review: Geekbench 7 single-core results

When it comes to Geekbench 7 single-core results, the 3,691 of the M5 Pro is similar to the M5 Max, since we are testing the fastest single core after all. They both lag behind the M6 Mac mini.

M5 Pro Mac mini review: Geekbench 7 multi-core results

When it comes to multi-core results a lot of this is down to sheer core counts for the CPU. Even though the M6 has the faster core, the M5 Pro goes ahead because it has 15 cores to the 12 in the M6.

Neither can compete with the M5 Max, because that has 18 CPU cores to play with.

M5 Pro Mac mini review: Geekbench 7 Metal results

On to graphics, and the M5 Pro's 121,303 is a very respectable score, though again we are dealing with a core count situation again. The lower-tier M5 Pro has a 16-cores GPU, while the M6 has 12 and the M5 Max has 32 cores.

There is one quirk worth knowing. The M5 Pro uses a single 16-core Neural Engine.

The cheaper base M6 has a dual Neural Engine. On that one metric, the M6 is better, but the M5 Pro answers with bandwidth and GPU cores. For most large local AI models, assuming that's what you're using the mini for, those matter more.

So "Pro" here means cores, bandwidth, and I/O. It does not mean the newest Neural Engine. And that's the side-step.

For most on-device machine learning and AI loads, the M6 is faster. Batch processing in Photos is faster, all other factors like SSD speed equal and so forth.

It's incredibly hard to make a universal statement about this, given the vagarities of how things are coded and so forth. This is something you probably need to test your own workflows before you buy, if you can.

The M5 Pro starts with 24GB of unified memory, versus the base M6 Mac mini's 16GB. That's a plus, and part of the steep starting price for the model.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: higher configurations will cost you

It configures up to 48GB or 64GB. The jump to 48GB adds $600 alone. Reaching 64GB costs $400 more on top of that.

Storage starts at 512GB, which is tight. Upgrades climb steeply, up to $3,800 for 8TB.

This is where the price ladder bites. A loaded mini passes entry-level Mac Studio money fast.

As part of that bite, the lowest configuration Mac mini M5 Pro unit has a slower, but not slow, SSD. That core configuration reads and writes at about 6600 megabytes per second

Jumping to that 1TB configuration, increases speed to about 10,800 megabytes per second read and write. This all comes down to parallelization, with the higher-end specs having multiple flash storage chips.

The M5 Pro's clearest win for users is Thunderbolt 5. Three Thunderbolt 5 ports sit on the back, with each hitting a peak speed with video connections of up to 120Gbps.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: Thunderbolt connectivity with Ethernet and HDMI

The base M6 mini stays on Thunderbolt 4. So this is a real reason to step up from the M6 Mac mini for Mac-bound workflows.

For fast external storage or docks, it matters, assuming you're Thunderbolt 5 ready.

There is also HDMI and 2.5Gb Ethernet. A 10Gb Ethernet upgrade is available, but again, watch those upgrade prices as you get close to Mac Studio territory.

There are no USB-A ports, as before. Everything modern runs through USB-C or Thunderbolt.

There are no surprises for speed on Thunderbolt.

The M5 Pro drives up to three external displays. The primary can reach 8K at 60Hz. It also handles 5K at 120Hz on that input. That covers demanding creative setups.

Wireless is current, with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Both match the rest of the 2026 line.

The M5 Pro mini lives in a tight spot. It sits between two tempting neighbors.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: a tough choice when Mac Studio exists

Below it is the base M6 mini at $899. That covers most everyday and even prosumer work. Adding $600 of upgrades gets you a better single-core speed for most tasks, and equivalent storage.

Above it is the M5 Max Mac Studio at $2,499. A loaded M5 Pro mini rapidly blows past that price, with the Studio getting you better cooling, far better I/O and more. And, we've seen this as low as $1999 at MicroCenter, assuming you have one near you.

So the sweet spot is a base or lightly upgraded config. Spec it moderately, and the Studio is right there.

The M5 Pro Mac mini packs real power in a small box. Thunderbolt 5 and strong multi-core are the draw.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: here for you if size is a concern for your desktop computer

It clearly outmuscles the base M6 mini. It also costs nearly twice as much.

The AI story is mixed, given the single Neural Engine. But bandwidth and GPU cores still help large models.

Buy it for Thunderbolt 5 and multi-core work. Just watch the upgrade ladder toward the Studio.

When the new machines launched, I considered a M6 Mac mini, the M5 Pro, and the M5 Max Mac Studio. The price ladder for M5 Pro didn't make a lot of sense to me, so I dismissed that one right away.

Mac mini M5 Pro review: an in-between option

Ultimately, I went for Mac Studio. The M5 Max versus M5 Pro performance paired with far better cooling drew me in. The six combined USB-C and Thunderbolt ports sealed the deal.

As such, I recommend a lightly-upgraded or core M6 for most Mac users with productivity workflows if you're not looking to spend Mac Studio money. If you're AI-oriented, the Mac Studio is a better choice.

The M5 Pro just sits in a funky spot. It's a good computer, maybe even a great one. Unfortunately, there are better options on both the lower and higher ends, granting better performance for the price you pay.

I like the M5 Pro Mac mini. In a vacuum, it's fantastic.

The M6 Mac mini versus M5 Pro Mac mini versus M5 Max Mac Studio are not spherical chickens in a vacuum. There are friction points with M5 Pro that cannot be ignored in the price to performance calculations.

This review covers the "entry-level" model if you can call it that at $1699. I prefer the $1099 M6 Mac mini configuration with more storage to the entry-level M5 Pro Mac mini.

The best deal in computing is no longer the Mac mini. The core Mac Studio at $2499 is the best choice of the three, with the best balance of features, performance, and cost, by far.

My workflows are not yours, though, with mine being calculation- and GPU-heavy and not AI-primary.

That said, I have talked to folks who are all-in on generative AI. They too prefer the Mac Studio M5 Max over the M5 Pro. There's more memory bandwidth, with more RAM at the "entry level," far better cooling, and more performance for about what they'd spend on an upgraded M5 Pro Mac mini

For us, the math is easy. It's M6 Mini with more storage on the inexpensive workhorse side, or Mac Studio with M5 Max for big iron, with the M5 Pro the odd-man out. For you, it may not be.

Apple's M5 Pro Mac mini starts at $1,699, but resellers Amazon and B&H Photo are already knocking $30 off the retail spec with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage at the time of this review.

The flow of leaks for the Apple-LG smart home collection is continuing to flow, with images of security cameras now surfacing.

Wednesday's news has been dominated by leaks surrounding smart home accessories co-developed by Apple and LG. After the first wave of image leaks for part of the range, there's now photographs of the cameras.

The post by @Ringo_tech on X depicts multiple cameras, including the LG Video Doorbell Wired, Floodlight Cam, Outdoor Cam Plug-In, and LG Indoor Cam Plug-In.

The LG Video Doorbell is a tubular device with both a main camera and a second downward-facing camera. It connects over Wi-Fi with support for 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands, with WPA2 and WPA3 security as well as Thread.

The Outdoor Cam Plug-in is a tubular device with a ball-joint mount. It has infrared LEDs for night-time shooting, as well as a microphone and speaker for two-way communication.

EXCLUSIVE

First look at LG's upcoming smart home lineup:

LG Video Doorbell Wired

LG Floodlight Cam

LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In

LG Indoor Cam Plug-In https://t.co/vblGECQLM1

Again, it supports dual-band Wi-Fi and Thread, but also NFC. As an outdoor camera, it has "waterproof grease" and O-rings to seal it up.

The LG Floodlight Cam is similar to the Outdoor Cam, in that it has infrared LEDs, a mic and speaker, and wireless connectivity including Wi-Fi, Thread, and NFC.

It also shares its design with the Outdoor Cam too, except it has two side tubes containing lamps.

Lastly, the LG Indoor Cam Plug-in is a camera on an arm, which can sit on a shelf. The leaker says it has a motor and gear mechanism for the vertical tilt mechanism, which may mean it can be moved by remote control.

It includes Hall IC components, as well as infrared LEDs and a mic and speaker. Wi-Fi support is also included, along with Thread and NFC.

The latest leak follows an earlier one that showed off the LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, the LG Smart Thermostat, and the LG Temperature Sensor.

As a whole, the collection of devices is believed to be a collaboration between Apple and LG. It is also thought that the range will be sold under the LG brand, much like the LG UltraFine Display, instead of bearing Apple's logo.

Current speculation is that LG will introduce the collection in 2027.

Muddying the waters is the long-standing rumor of Apple working on its own privacy-centric smart home camera system, separate from its work with LG.

On a podcast, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman described Apple's device as a cylinder that looks like a "metal giant chapstick." One or two of the leaked LG products somewhat match that description.

Apple is also expected to reveal new smart home products on October 13. The candidates include the long-awaited Home Hub, as well as updates to the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini.
